title: Levi Yitzchak, the people's lawyer
hook: Levi Yitzchak's commentary finds merit in the people in every portion
tomorrow: a prayer that asks to see people's virtues, not their faults?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rabbi's son: delays that looked like signs, until it was too late. Don't wait too long. Today, a rabbi who never ran out of reasons to defend people.

Every group chat has the friend nobody appointed: the one who says, wait, maybe she didn't see the message. Every single time. Hasidic stories have a friend like that at the level of heaven: Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, remembered as the defender of Israel, who argued the people's case before God. One story people tell: he sees a man greasing the wheels of his wagon while still wrapped in his tallit and tefillin, mid-prayer. Anyone else might scold him. Levi Yitzchak looks up and says: Master of the world, look at Your people. Even while they grease their wheels, they pray to You.
screen: `MAYBE SHE DIDN'T SEE THE MESSAGE.` → `THE DEFENDER OF ISRAEL.` → `EVEN GREASING WHEELS, THEY PRAY.`

segments.voice: Under the story sits one question: when someone falls short, which way do you lean? Jewish teaching has an old answer in Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers: judge every person l'chaf zechut, toward the scale's pan of merit. Levi Yitzchak lived that out loud. His commentary on the weekly Torah portions, the Kedushat Levi, is remembered for finding merit in the people, portion after portion, and in the stories he takes their side even with God. Always the merit. Now a neighbor tradition, in its own words. In Paul's first letter to the Corinthians, a chapter on love says, in the King James Version, that charity, meaning love, "thinketh no evil," and "Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things." Two old traditions, side by side: before you settle on the worst, look for the good reading of a person. That's real shared ground. And the honest difference. Paul calls it love, and ends the chapter, "the greatest of these is charity." The Mishnah's word is judgment, a fair scale, tipped kindly. And Levi Yitzchak often turns the merit upward, as a plea: he stands before God as the people's lawyer. One describes how love sees a neighbor; the other also argues the neighbor's case in heaven. Neither is a copy of the other. Both lean the same way.
screen: `WHICH WAY DO YOU LEAN?` · `JUDGE TOWARD MERIT.` · `LOVE THINKETH NO EVIL.` · `A LAWYER BEFORE GOD.` · then, large: `JUDGE EVERY PERSON TOWARD MERIT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who let you down this week in a small way. In your notes app, or as a real message, write them a few lines that start from the most generous reading of what happened. You don't have to send it; for the rest of the sit, just read it back slowly and see how it sits.
screen: `ONE SMALL LETDOWN.` · `THE MOST GENEROUS READING.` · `READ IT BACK.`

segments.voice: Always the merit: Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev's way. Judge every person toward merit, and when it counts, argue their case.
Your line: judge every person toward merit, the good reading before the worst one. Shalom for now.

howItsDone: Jews learn the teaching to judge others favorably, dan l'chaf zechut, from Pirkei Avot, often studied on Shabbat afternoons; Levi Yitzchak's Kedushat Levi is studied on the weekly Torah portion, and stories of him pleading for the people are told especially around the High Holy Days.
